blocks.x: Well, we forgot about Lytel and Frankie Signorelli. About 1920, Signorelli joined my band. At that time they may have had a Memphis Five, but I never heard of them stopping the machine. Well, I had a little bit of friction with Roberson. He had promised the band a thousand dollars if I put Margie over. Well, I saw the plug of Margie for him, sang it for him, placed it on the record for him, and after he got his first statement, he didn't say anything. I asked him about what he was going to do to three of them. That was Conrad and Benny Davis, and he, what he gave us, a thousand dollars for plugging his tune. I was in the band business to make money. I wasn't out just to play somebody's number when I had other numbers of my own, unless I was going to get something out of them. So it was promised by the three of us we were to get this money, and I asked Roberson for the money. He didn't say nothing. He just ignored me, just kept on playing his piano. The next day I gave him his two weeks' notice, and I replaced him. This was at the Follinsbergine with Frank Signorelli, who I had tried out in a song plugger's place, or in other words, a publisher's place. In that time they had little rooms where you could go in and listen to music. Well this boy knew all our numbers from the recordings, and he was a very good pianist, and he had got the rhythm down pretty good. And we hired him. Frankie stood with me from 1920, part of 1920, 21, and 22. We went to Balconnates, and after about six or eight weeks there I became ill with the flute. And I pulled the band out. It was here that the Memphis Five got their foothold on Broadway through the efforts of Frank Signorelli, and Jimmy Lytel, who had replaced Shields after Shields thought he had enough money and left the band. And I don't know where he went, whether he went to Chicago, California, I don't know. I have never corresponded with him at any time since then. It was here that the Memphis Five got the job at the Balconnates. But prior to that they had made recordings for Sam Lanham, and the lads, seven black aces or something on that order. And they had copied every arrangement. Through Frank Signorelli, he knew the arrangements, how we played them, and from this clarinet player. It was easy for Philly Napoleon and the rest of them, like Nick Moore, to fall in line on these arrangements, because the piano player had learned them. And that was the beginning of the Memphis Five big history in the world. I remember when Philly Napoleon came to me around 1918, he used to beg me to show him how to make slurs in different passages on the clarinet. That's before I knew they had a Memphis Five. And I used to help him out. I helped a fellow named Frank Garanti. I helped Big Spider-Vac. In fact, I started him on the trumpet, Big Spider-Vac. I was a kid. Many people said it's not so. But this boy came to New York when he was 17 years of age. And he wouldn't let him in, Rising Webbers. He was too young. And he told the doorkeeper, because Rising Webbers at this time was a 400 club. You couldn't get in there unless you had a pass. And there was a dollar cover charge. It's the only place that had a dollar cover charge on Broadway. And you had to be exclusive to come into that room. And we played. We played in there since 1917, January 15 or 17 we opened there. But we was in New York before January 15 because we didn't have tuxedos to open there. We had to go get tuxedos, photographs and stuff. We were in a big time there. And in our first two weeks' tryout they tried us in the paradise. Some of the ads in the paper might spell J-A-S-Z. Some of them spell J-A-S. Some is J-A-S-S. And some is J-A-Z-Z. While it was in Webbers. And the kind of people who visited that place was all the great actors like Charlie Chaplin, all many, every big star that played on Broadway. And Franklin Simons spent money in there like water. The Gould family. It was an exclusive room at Joanna. We were given a thousand dollars a week. When we made, on our collections, in the kiddie box that we used to have called a sugar can, sometime a hundred to two hundred dollars per night. They may dispute me on this but this is the truth. Now, if these bands in New Orleans existed, with all this loot going around, giving out in New York, and men like Ted Lewis, Ross Garner, Lopez, Vincent Lopez, former jazz bands, who copied after the style of the original Dixieland jazz bands recording, replacing these Negroes that had full sway because when we arrived there, Broadway was black. They had no white bands hardly at all playing on Broadway. They were all Negroes playing what they call syncopated or ragtime music. Now they say this music didn't exist anywhere else but New York, but it did. Because the way I copied from the records from Susan, others copied the same. There was no difference. Because I had read that article that someone sent me, that Louis Armstrong had an arm full of records and he was listening to them, and he copied from them. And nobody can tell me these other niggas didn't copy from them. If there's so many white men copied from the recordings of this band, which I'm going to try to play if we have enough time today, how these idioms got into this music. Going back to the Memphis Five, we used to play a tune called, Shemmy Like My Sister Kate, that A.J. P. Ronge sent to me. If my talk ain't chronological, I can't help it because my mind don't work like an educated man. I'm only telling you from heart. I have no script in front of you. I'll ask you, do I read from a script?

You don't see anything in front of me that I take notes from, only just from what comes to my mind. That's why I don't have it in chronological order. I can only tell you what I can think of at the time. Maybe my talk may be gobbled up a little bit, that I might put this one before the other one, the other one before the other one. But I am telling you the true facts of this music. It was in Chicago where I changed the rhythm. They had a certain dance team. They were doing a castle walk. And up in the north, people were doing a different step than they were doing a two-step in New Orleans. Here they did a skip step, which is called a two-step. Over there they did more like a walking step. After the first two numbers I played, maybe you won't believe that I was a good dancer. Maybe nobody vouched for that either because many of the men of my age that would know about me are dead. But I can tell you that nobody could beat me dancing. I don't give a darn. Whether they come from New York, Chicago, Paris, anywhere else on a dance floor. But with a rehearse dance they may be. But I say if I grabbed any individual girl that I danced better with her, then them professionals could. Because I had a way of making them follow the way I'd want them to go. In other words, a strong lead. Getting back to this rhythm, I noticed that they made a walk step. I said, we ain't going to go here, to myself. I told the drummer, I said, look, let's play this march. Slow it down. And we played a march like I played in street parades in New Orleans. And we slowed it down. From then on. Then we played other numbers in the same rhythm, syncopation, which was a different syncopation than the ragtime. Ragtime was jumping syncopation. Here again they'll dispute me. It says syncopation is all alike. But I say it is not. Because you could write syncopation of ragtime and you couldn't write these syncopated jazz names that we made. There would have to be a choir listening to a recording. Now each time a man listened to that record and he made this lick, he naturally would try to capture the way we played it. But not being one of us, it would come out his way. It would be a little different. But to me, I could feel that was what he was trying to play. One man on top of the other, they start putting these licks together. One, then two, then three, then four. They even included the endings of our tune. There's a lick. That's the ending. And they start and so on and down until they had them all together. But many people say, well why did I do that? Well my limited knowledge of music at that time, which is probably the same, I don't think I've progressed much more, yet I've heard them play, and I wouldn't still put them that way again because to me melody is music. Not a lot of noise and rhythm or background which you can play against supposed melody. It wouldn't be music. Because if you played one tune with the same background, you played the other one, they were the same. You must define that thing as melody. That was the reason why when I went to England, that's a foreign country. A lot of these guys said they went before us, they were too soon. The people didn't understand their music. They didn't have what it took to make them understand. Because if they had, they would have been known. And I never have been known in this world. I'd been still here with a pair of pliers, pulling on electric wires and connecting electric wires up like I used to do in my youth. But it looked like God put us together. And we were the only five that played this type of music. And I have never heard of a band. They have tried to imitate us, tried to play the way we played, but they never could play in unison. They took this stuff and played chorus by chorus. One man playing one chorus, one playing another. But they embodied the licks of the Dixieland Jazz band. And they played the licks of the chorus. So I never called that anything at all because any man plays one chorus in a tune and actually when he got to the end of the tune he was strong. If any cornet player is listening to me he'll know what I mean. But if he's not a cornet player he wouldn't understand me. Because when you knock off and you carry the ball and you pull it, you drive it all the way. You don't have time to run sidetrack or jump a curve or go this way or that way like these fellas have. They made it easy for themselves. In other words I'd call them one chorus men. They don't play the way we play. They play some of the idioms. They've contracted them, they've made them larger, yes. But they haven't improved any of them. And the rhythm they use, as long as they use it, that's Dixieland rhythm. And no one else will tell me it's different until they change that rhythm. Now, then I say they're playing different American music. That is what's embodied in American music. It's the recordings of the Dixieland jazz band. The writers have always said this rhythm came from Africa. Yet when it was brought to Africa these Negroes didn't know anything about it. They liked it, but they never knew nothing about it. It was tried on them. Now 40 years have passed, almost going on to 50 years. These Negroes are being civilized. They live in big towns, they work in big towns. They may have come in contact with this music since then. I don't say colored men can't play music because in 40 years they have did a lot of advancing in their music. But you've got to run to the facts as this. I'm talking about the early Negroes. They couldn't play a dance, nothing. They couldn't play nothing. And I mean what I say. Outside of a few bands that read music, many of them were taught by white men how to read that music and play. And they played the same ragtime as they played in the North because it was all scored music. That's P. Ron, Robichaud, and this fellow played a cornerhead of brass band, Manuel Perez. Now they played conventional music. I could show you on a record here a white man playing Too Much Mustard, Prince's Band. And I'd show you Jim Europe who was a colored man playing. And they both have the same rhythm. It's the same tune as written. They're playing for music. They had fake bands in my days, plenty of them. And every band, I'm going way back now because I think this is very interesting. And every band, the cornerhead player, carried a melody and he was the leader. Now you hear men today playing a bass or drums telling you what they played. They ain't played nothing. Because what they played was nothing but accompaniment. The man who played that harp styled that band. If he was a clarinet and he carried a melody, he was styling the band. Because when he hit his two licks with his foot down, and he gave the notes that he was the player what tune he was to play, or he either told them what number he was going to play, and if it was a strange band he'd tell them the key he was going to play in. So they'd know. And he'd hit the two licks and they all hit simultaneously, go together. Now many bands were all carnet bands. They didn't know harmony. Many of them used to play bass on the trombone, what they called a vamp style. Vamp style is nothing but boop, boop, boop, boop, bass. Why they did that? Because they didn't know how to put the trombone. Just like when I put the rooster crow in there, I didn't know what the hell to put in there. So I was a fake and I went, eeeeee. I didn't know what to put in there. I wasn't educated in music that I could pick up a rhyme out of some book somewhere and slip it in there like the men today can do. They can go to work and what they'll learn is exercises. If they hit a chord, they know what the chord is. They'll run an exercise or something and put it in their own way. But I didn't have that. I didn't have that knowledge. And that's why all this humbug came up. The flutter tongue come in when I used to hear these guys triple tongue. Is that flutter tongue? No, that's just a common man trying to cover up like a cat would do his dirt. I didn't know any better. And that's why that come about. Later, the good musicians use it today. It's high class today. It's not low class. In my time they used to throw rocks, potatoes, and anything they could get at me. And the men of the boys that are talking today used to come where I used to play with these string bands and throw at the house where I was playing because they thought I was lousy. Because what I played was different than they played. I was thrown on my own to compose my tunes. I told you how I composed several other tunes. And most of the tunes that I have ever composed came that way. I used to go to a show, listen to the tune. Come back that night I couldn't play it. That night laying in bed this tune would come to me. Some of it anyway. The next day I'd come on the job I'd say to Regis, I'd say, run this over. I'd get the chords on the piano. I'd say run this over. I think I've got the melody on this tunes we went to last night. And the people would ask for me advice and weapons I didn't know. So if I knew the first four or five bars in the chord construction, that's all I wanted. And when I played them, they were not like the tune that I had to wait. Maybe the four or five bars that I could commit to memory was mostly exactly the same. But I'll bet you the rest wasn't because I didn't know the melody and I'd fake it. I'd put different licks and different other things in there to fit the chord construction. Those people went wild. They thought that was the greatest thing that ever happened. They never heard music played like that before. How could they hear music? Because whenever they went there they would have men played by music. They didn't hear no impromptu or improvisation on any tune. Speaking of rising weathers I played there 112 weeks consecutively. And we never made less than $250 and we made as high as $300 a week counting our collections. There's nobody that ever lived that ever played that much. Besides we played all the theaters around New York in conjunction with rising members. Outside of that sign we were billed as the creators of jazz. And that's where we were taking that point from that on. And in the contract you'll find that we played exclusive music. That we were playing with the other songs. And you'll see in paragraphs one of us had dropped out the band. They could sue the rest of us for damages that's being done because our rhythm was different than any other band that ever had to foreplayed or ever played. And rising weathers tried out many bands to try to get their expenses down. I had told you about these negros coming up to New York. They played for Gloria Goodwin and this fellow Webb. I always get Jack Webb but it ain't Jack Webb. It's another Webb. They did a dancing act for this Dolodrina at the Moomont. They stayed almost two weeks. They went into Vaudeville. And when they write about them they say they had an extended engagement. Let me tell you the extended engagement they had. They extended them out the back door. That's the extended engagement they had. And the item, and I mean the variety, I've already mentioned that again, I'm going to tell you again. You read it March the 10th, that every band on Broadway that played or supposed to play jazz was classed as imitators. I have never kept anybody from getting a job on Broadway. In fact, I sent for boys. I helped them out to get jobs. Many of them I got out of jail for no visible means of support. We put them on there and paid their way back to New Orleans so they could go back and work. Would it be good taste for me to mention some of them guys? Sure, go right ahead, huh? Well, I'll tell you one was Eddie Rowland. He came up there with Tom Brown's reorganized band. And after Tom Brown and them went back, I don't know where they went to New Orleans or Chicago, I had given money to several of their members, fair, because they couldn't get a job. They tried out at Healy's. This is in the early part of the jazz business. They played there one night and they never let them finish the night. They let them go. Their music was no different than other music that was being played around. They found no difference in them because they never made a hit and they didn't get the job. They tried out at Rice and Weathers. And their agent told them you could put these men behind a crate and you wouldn't know the difference between these boys and the original Dixieland jazz band. Well, I lived around the corner at the Punchet Train Hotel it was called, man. And I came by and as I came by the bartender said, give me a notice to come on in. He said, go upstairs and listen. He said, some guys are trying to get you down. I went and I stayed in the lobby and I heard them play a number. And they tried to play some numbers that belonged to me. Mr. Wagner and Mr. Schultz, the manager, walked out on them while they were playing the first number. That's where Tom Brown says he played at Rice and Weathers. He tried out at Rice and Weathers but he didn't have a job there. That I had positive because I was there for three years. And no other band played there but our band. Now, they come to New Orleans and they tell different stories. I'll tell you how the stories thought. I had began to tell you about Marshall Stein's story. How he started up all this to put the Negros in. Well, this man comes from Columbia University where most of them all taught pro-criminalists and Negro integration. Most of the only guys that come out there, you'll find them in LSU and many other places. They were learned at Columbia University. That's the heartbeat. Marshall Stein's right now holds a position up there. He came down to New Orleans and he sold them a bill of goods to Myra Menville and Dr. Sushant. He said, well, they may be intelligent people. They may be smarter than I am because they have set up what you call a racket to form a jazz club to disseminate or put liars out in the public. Untruths, all written by Negroes who did nothing or created nothing in this music in the days and God knows where they played. But their word is more truth than mine who have made history and has the proof to back up this historical part that the original Dixieland jazz band made. I'd like to read your letter. I'll let you read it but the way you put all these dots and dashes in there, if you'll eliminate them dots and dashes. I'll let him read it. I'd like you to read this here. This was for the celebration of the introduction of jazz into England in 1990 by the one and only original Dixieland jazz band led by Nick LaRocca. This article appeared in the States paper in regards to me having an invitation to go to England for the commemoration of this affair. Would you kindly take your time and read down? This is Miss Bendel's letter. This is LaValle.
Can you hold it a second?

Pioneer of jazz wins recognition, New Orleans, editor from New Orleans States. It was gratifying to read in your paper on February 27th the article on Nick LaRocca, famous leader of the original Dixieland jazz band. He deserves the honor accorded him and his band by the Jazz Club of England whose leader, Marcus O'Donoghau visited our sea last summer. If Mr. LaRocca accepts this invitation, and I hope he does, I'm sure he will mention some of the other bands that played jazz at that time. Tom Brown, who took his group to Chicago a few months before the original Dixieland jazz band arrived there, and was billed as Tom Brown and his Dusters while playing at the Lambs Cafe, the original Creole band with Buddy Bolden, Freddie Keppert, George Bakke, and others. left here in 1911. Clarence Williams, Bunk Johnson, Sidney Bechet, and Kit Aurey had gone from here by 1913. And there was Oscar Papaselestine too, who is still playing music that the tourists come to New Orleans to hear. Everybody knows, of course, about Jack Lane's band. It has been said that nearly all the white musicians in New Orleans played in his bands at one time or another. There was Johnny Fishers, Al Seed Yellow Nunezes, Bill Galates, and so many other bands. These pioneers deserve recognition. They gave us the great American music called Excellente Jazz, which is sweeping the country again. Publicity in national magazines shows definitely that the current revival of the music is due to a great extent to the efforts of the New Orleans Jazz Club during the past two years. Incidentally, Tom Brown is a member of our club, as well as Tony Spargo, who played drums in Mr. LaRocca's famous band. He was now with Bill Napoleon's Jazz Band in New York City. Too often, recognition and praise come too late. We are glad this is not so in Mr. LaRocca's case. We want to thank the New Orleans States for the interview with me. This is Myra Vanville, Secretary of New Orleans Jazz Club.

I'd like to comment on the dates that she has here to show you she was eaten up, taken in by this communist propaganda. I wish you'd hear this tape recorder. Buddy Bolin, Freddie Kepler, George Pequet left here in 1911. In 1906, by the things that I have in my hand, from Louisiana State Mental Hospital at Jackson, Louisiana, Bolin was incarcerated in there in 1906. He couldn't have played with them. And I've told you when these Negroes came it was 1917. Clarence Williams, he says, left here around 1911 or 13. Clarence Williams would only be 13 years of age. He was still in the country, in Plaquemine, Louisiana. This Negro could be around the age of Armstrong. He could be no more than 58, right now if he's living. Same as Armstrong. And none of them heard Buddy Bolin play. I am going on 70 and I never knew nothing about this Negro Bolin until he's history and started digging from Negro mythology and tales that I don't know where they get him. But did they hear what he played? That's the question. No. They didn't hear what he played. Now they want me to mention Fisher. Now Johnny Fisher brought his band to New York. He was a failure. In his band he played the clarinet. He had George Voth playing the clarinet. He had Happy Shilling playing trombone. And he had several other members that I just don't recall at this present time. And they didn't even secure a job. They tried out all over New York. And they came back on their ears. I don't know whether they rode back the rails or walked home. Now I'm to mention these people. They wouldn't ask Jimmy Durante to mention me that I got him his first jazz band and helped him to put it together. And from that he made his success. They wouldn't ask him that question. But they'll ask me to mention these people who have never made history. This woman must think I was a fool or some other sort of that. Had these men that went before me. If this be true. Then to them I say again would have been the glory. And not to Nick LaRocca's band. That made the success. Sometime later she's supposed to have sent me a letter. Stop that machine.
In this letter. In this letter. In this letter.

You asked me that I forgot to say who replaced Lytel and Signorelli. Two New York boys, they were both from Brooklyn. One was Artie Seboyg and the other was Henry Vanacella. He played the flam net and Vanacella played the piano. Now, each change I made, I didn't come to New Orleans. Although I was relegated in a dance hall.
What about Signer Running? You say he made some records.

Oh yes, he recorded with us in the latter part of our contact with the victim. The numbers offhand I can't tell you, but if you look through the files, you'll find out I have letters that I sent to this Brian Russ, and I tell him about the men who played on the recording.

After I came back to New Orleans, I laid around a little while before I'd go back into the building business, building houses and repair. I sent to Wilson Hotel, which was the same punchy trade hotel, now it's called Wilson, for my trunk. I found out it had...

segments.chapter: Original Dixieland Jazz Band in New York
segments.title: Signorelli, Memphis Five, and Reisenweber's Broadway years
segments.summary: La Rocca recalls the Margie plug dispute, hiring Frank Signorelli, how the Memphis Five copied the band's arrangements, and the 1917 Reisenweber's engagement, money and clientele.

segments.title: Rhythm, syncopation and imitators of the Dixieland band
segments.summary: He says he changed the rhythm in Chicago, defends his band's unison style against one-chorus imitators, and argues early Black bands only played scored ragtime. He also describes faking tunes, Reisenweber's pay, rival bands and Marshall Stearns.

segments.title: Reading Myra Menville's letter on New Orleans bands
segments.summary: The interviewer reads a letter to the editor from the New Orleans Jazz Club secretary listing early New Orleans bands and musicians who deserve recognition.

segments.title: La Rocca disputes the letter's dates and band claims
segments.summary: He rejects the letter's dates for Bolden and Clarence Williams, dismisses Johnny Fisher's New York failure, and resents being asked to name other bands.

segments.title: Later band replacements and Signorelli's recordings
segments.summary: He names Seboyg and Vanacella as replacements for Lytel and Signorelli, then answers a question about Signorelli's recordings with the band and his letters to Brian Rust.

segments.title: Returning to New Orleans and the building trade
segments.summary: After coming back to New Orleans he went back to building and repairing houses and sent for his trunk from the hotel; the transcript breaks off.
